## 要点

**Tom Milton:** Your most likely route to the Nobel Prize for making AI go well is that you are the one who develops the verification tools that enable a deal.

**Tom Reed:** You would need to retrofit like every single data centre in China and every data centre in the US — like it just seems to me like it would require a level of cooperation that’s completely impossible.

**Tom Milton:** When I speak to my non-AI friends about this, they kind of say, “Why can’t you just turn it off?” And you do always have this fallback that you could turn data centres off. We could turn all data centres off in the world, but that’s extremely costly. Lots of what verification is doing is reducing the costs to complying with some kind of slowdown.

**Tom Reed:** Just by looking at the power, you can be like, “OK, great: there’s no backwards passes happening here”?

**Tom Milton:** So as the power is being used, it fluctuates. So you can see all of these little spikes, the really small ones. That happens at the start of each layer. A marginal really talented AI safety researcher could have a huge impact on verification. I think if you started on this today, by the end of the year, you’d probably be one of the best like five people in the world working on verification, or one of the most useful five people in the world.

**Tom Reed:** Today I’m speaking with Tom Milton, who is the CEO of Amodo Design , which is a company that builds hardware for scientific research, biosecurity, and AI verification . And it is, above all, the last of these that I’m interested in talking about with you today, because I feel like the problem you’re trying to solve is both very hard and very, very important. Pretty much anytime I look at AI news, it looks to me like there is another lab CEO, or another letter signed by thousands of employees, insisting that they want to slow down the progress of AI development , but that they are personally unable to do so for fear of losing the frontier or ceding the frontier to either another American company or, really, in the long term, China. And it feels like so much of what we would want to do on AI safety in basically any capacity is bottlenecked on this ability to trust that if everyone wants to slow down, the other actors are in fact also slowing down. At Amodo, you are building tech which would allow us to do this. Could you tell me exactly how this tech might work?

**Tom Milton:** Absolutely. We’ll start by setting aside the fact that I think a unilateral slowdown could also be good. We’ll go on from here assuming that people are shooting for multilateral actions. When we think about a slowdown, the problem is trust, and therefore the problem is knowing what is happening at another AI developer, whether it’s a country or a company. And we can then break that down into some of the inputs of development. You could think about the employees as one input; you think about the software, algorithms, and data; you could then also think about the compute. And we’re focused on the compute. This is the physical chips that AI development and deployment runs on. And this is a really attractive place to do our verification — to do our checking whether someone is slowing down — because they are very specialised to the AI setting. You need many thousands of them, and at least for now, they all need to be in the same location. So it’s a great place to start for monitoring what different parties are doing on AI.

**Tom Reed:** And so you’re building ways that you could look at compute and make claims that would be verifiable by someone else about what that compute is being used for. What kinds of claims would you be aiming to verify?

**Tom Milton:** Exactly. So you’ve said the word “claims” there. To explain a bit of language at the top: we say there is a ‘prover’ who makes a claim, and a ‘verifier’ who then checks that claim.

**Tom Reed:** Right, so the prover could be an AI company.

**Tom Milton:** Exactly. It could be an AI company, whether that’s controlled by a country or not — essentially the developer. And then the verifier: this could be another country, it could be a third party, whether it’s an embedded auditor or international organisation. And the claims that people want to verify depend kind of on what your goals are. So recent examples might be OpenAI claiming that they have stopped training after their latest RL [reinforcement learning] accidents. So you might want to verify the claim, “We are not doing any reinforcement learning inside our company.” And as AI safety science advances, I think we’ll have more specific claims that we want to verify.So right now we can say this data centre is on or off: there is no AI activity happening, or there is some. Or we might want to go all the way through to details like: this safety training technique has to happen, or this type of training technique is too dangerous and we promise we’re not doing it. Or these data were held out, or we are or aren’t using neuralese. But most of that requires the science of AI development to…

**Tom Reed:** To understand which claims you would want to be able to make to begin with.

**Tom Milton:** Exactly.

**Tom Reed:** And so the verification R&D process is allowing us to make more and more fine-grained claims, so we’re not stuck at this very costly level of, “The data centre is literally off, and therefore I know for sure there’s no training happening there.”

**Tom Milton:** Yeah. When I speak to my non-AI friends about this, they kind of say, “Why can’t you just turn it off?” And you do always have this fallback that you could turn data centres off. We could turn all data centres off in the world, but that’s extremely costly. Inference is valuable, providing access to the models is valuable. And lots of what verification is doing is reducing the cost to complying with some kind of slowdown. So at first it might be turning the data centre on and off, then it might be serving only inference — and being able to prove you’re only serving inference allows you to still serve inference whilst being worried that training would be dangerous and should be stopped. Then we might want to do something like resume small-scale AI safety experiments — alignment experiments, for example. And this is where beginning to make more and more precise claims about how compute is being used is more and more useful. It both reduces the cost to coming to a deal, but also opens up a bunch of value for humanity in still being able to use the compute for something and still being able to use the AIs for something.

**Tom Reed:** Great. Let’s zoom in on this example of trying to verify someone’s claims that they’re using a given data centre to do inference and not to do training. And you can imagine this being useful if OpenAI wanted to verify to someone that they had in fact paused a training run, or you could imagine it to be useful in some grander scenario where the US and China have agreed to pause training for some amount of time. AI 2040: Plan A imagines this kind of thing. From what I understand, you’ve built a prototype that is working towards this, that could verify that a small cluster of GPUs is in fact being used for inference and not training. Could you, at a high level, walk me through how that would work?

**Tom Milton:** So we’ve got a pilot of a system that uses what we call “ inference recomputation .” If you were thinking about monitoring the compute, you could go all the way down to the GPU level, and you could try and look at the instructions that are running on the GPU. We operate at a slightly higher level so that it’s less invasive, and we look at the network traffic. So there’s this front-end network connecting the GPUs to each other and also to the outside world. And we look at the information on that network, we install a network certifier — what this basically does is forward on the information to our verifier node; the information still goes on to its original destination, it’s just duplicated — and then on the verifier we run a recomputation. You can think about this as simply rerunning the inference that happened. So normally your input tokens go into your model, you do your inference, and you get your output tokens. What we are doing is then feeding those through the model again and checking whether they came out the same. And this allows us to look at the front-end network, look at the information on that network, and confirm whether or not it came from the model that we all agreed should be running. And of course there’s some nondeterminism in these models. You need to account for this. We use an algorithm called DiFR that looks at some of the probability of choosing different tokens, and on a long section of text can have quite high confidence as to whether these tokens did indeed come from the right model.

**Tom Reed:** And if no training is happening, then that model is staying constant, and therefore you know that it’s only doing inference, because otherwise the model would be changing over time?

**Tom Milton:** Yeah, so the model staying constant is one thing. The other thing is there aren’t packets, bits of information on that network that can’t be explained by the recomputation. So another way of describing this is bounding the unexplained communication. If you can explain all of the communication that’s happening, then you can know that all of that comes from the agreed inference. If there is this unexplained information on the network, then there is a workload that you don’t know about happening.

**Tom Reed:** Interesting. OK, yeah. So just to lay this out again: you’re claiming to me, “Here’s the set of GPUs that I have, here’s the model that I’m serving on these GPUs to these customers. And you’re going to be able to trust me, because you are going to have a part within my data centre where you can rerun the model that I’m claiming I’m using, and it will produce the same tokens as the ones that are actually being sent to external users. And in addition to that, I can also put network taps into your server, and they will also be able to certify that there’s no other things going on other than the inference that I’m also able to recompute.” Is that correct as a summary? Have I missed anything?

**Tom Milton:** Yeah, so you’re coming in to check me —

**Tom Reed:** Let’s say I’m the verifier, yeah.

**Tom Milton:** You’re going to put in your server that does the rerunning. The network tap — “tap” stands for “test access point” — is a piece of fairly standard data centre networking equipment. And all that’s going to do is forward the packets on to the verifier. So this is the piece of equipment that basically bridges your verifier hardware to my prover hardware. And the main thing that you’re going to do when you come in is install that tap to forward the packets on to you, so you get a copy of them as well as me having my original copy of them.

**Tom Reed:** And you’ve built a small-scale version of this and it works. So I would be able to run this, and whatever you’re running on your GPU, I don’t need to look into your GPU in any kind of invasive level of detail. I can just look at what my own recomputation is providing, and I can be certain that you’re running the model that you’re claiming.

**Tom Milton:** Yes, exactly.

**Tom Reed:** What scale does this work at?

**Tom Milton:** So we’ve got this running on about 30, 32 H100s, H200s at our demo research cluster in Sheffield.

**Tom Reed:** Great. OK, that’s cool. And are you hoping that this basic prototype would be the kind of thing that could be used in a deal between the US and China? I mean, this strikes me as requiring quite a lot of mutual trust. I need to trust that when I’m putting my server within your data centre, you’re not then tampering with it. You need to trust that the network taps that I’m putting in your data centre, they’re not somehow picking up on IP that you don’t want to give to me. Am I right in thinking this requires a lot of mutual trust?

**Tom Milton:** So I think the things that get implemented in future deals are likely to, rather than relying on recomputation, end up relying on zero-knowledge proofs .

**Tom Reed:** Where recomputation is the part where I rerun the model weights.

**Tom Milton:** Exactly. And the important part of this is that rerunning meant that I had to have access to the model weights as the verifier. You’re the verifier; you had to have access to my model. And it was within the security boundary; it was within my data centre, so I had some confidence over the security of the model. I was fairly sure that by putting it within my walls, you weren’t stealing the model. But we would much prefer if I didn’t have to share the model with you at all. And the way we can do this is with zero-knowledge proofs. And there are a few teams already working on this. We’re working to implement this.

**Tom Reed:** This is ongoing work. There’s not an established way to do this?

**Tom Milton:** Well, there are some established zero-knowledge machine learning approaches. The main problem with what’s kind of referred to as ZKML, or zero-knowledge proofs for inference, is that they’re really slow.

**Tom Reed:** They’re very computationally demanding. There’s a lot of overhead.

**Tom Milton:** Many orders of magnitude more computational overhead to run using the zero-knowledge approach. Although this is coming down, and seems like something that actually you could hill-climb with the AIs quite effectively. The reason I’m hopeful on implementing the type of system we’re talking about is that we don’t need to check every single packet on the network. So although it may be thousands of times slower to generate this proof, actually only checking one in 1,000 gives us some reasonable confidence.

**Tom Reed:** There’s a way you can sample some of the packets that are being sent around without having to do it with every single one, and you know that they’re not spoofing you in some way.

**Tom Milton:** Exactly. Yeah, subsampling. And the fraction you need to sample is roughly on the game theory you expect of their cheating, and how worried they’d be about being caught, and the probability of getting caught. So right now a few of our team are implementing some of these zero-knowledge proofs on top of the prototype I just described, so that rather than having a recomputation server, that verification server is running some of this zero-knowledge system, and therefore the prover doesn’t need to share the model weights with the verifier. And that’s going to be much more palatable on an international scheme.

**Tom Reed:** Great, great. And as I understand it, this is just one of the ways you could verify — you’re looking at a specific type of information, you’re looking at the network traffic or whatever, to understand what a data centre is being used for. But I believe we have here with us a prop in the studio which tries to establish the same thing — AKA that inference and not training is happening — by looking at the power that is consumed by a data centre. Could you walk me through exactly how that works? And for our audio listeners, we have a prop here. You can follow along on video if you want to see exactly what it looks like, but we’ll do our best to describe it in the requisite level of detail.

**Tom Milton:** Yeah. In addition to monitoring the network, there are a bunch of other physical things we could try and monitor about a data centre and about compute. One would be how the memory is being used: doing random challenges to see what’s in memory and then correlate that to a workload. We can generate these zero-knowledge proofs. We could do something like proof of work, which gives you cryptographic proofs that all of the GPU’s resources are being consumed. And then another thing we can do is monitor something like power. So the GPU is drawing a lot of power. We all know that data centres use lots of power, but as the power is being used, it fluctuates: the power consumption of the compute changes with the operations that it’s doing. So in this box here we have a kind of mock setup of a simple server tray. We have an Nvidia GPU, a Blackwell series GPU, and the hardware that’s part of the verification here is this small inductive loop. So this is wrapped around the power supply to the GPU. And then we can see on our oscilloscope here how the power is fluctuating over time. So we’ve got time on x, and current on y. And you can see firstly a forward pass, and then a backwards pass, and then a break.

**Tom Reed:** So what are we running on this? What did we run on this GPU?

**Tom Milton:** I think we ran nanoGPT or something — GPT-2 or something like this. And you can see actually a bunch of properties just from the power consumption. You can see all of these little spikes, the really small ones — that happen at the start of each layer, and you can actually tell this is a 12-layer model from those spikes. You see there’s a lot of information that leaks out of this. In the field of security, these are referred to as side channels or covert communication channels. There are all sorts of crazy ways that nation-states and other hackers use these to steal information. But we can also use these as a way to monitor the workloads that are happening.

**Tom Reed:** And the idea here is that the amount of power that a given GPU or even a whole data centre is drawing when it’s doing a certain action — like a backwards pass — is distinguishable enough from a forwards pass that just by looking at the power, you can be like, “OK, great, there’s no backwards pass happening here.” Is that correct?

**Tom Milton:** It’s kind of fingerprinting. Workloads have fingerprints. They have communication patterns you see on the networks; they have power patterns as well. And we might not be able to, at a whole data centre level, tell this is definitely a backwards pass, but there are fluctuations that are canonical — they’re kind of representative, or are often a fingerprint of doing different workloads. And another kind of easy example here is that if you go and read news reports about frontier data centres, you’ll read about all of these grid problems that happen where there are these really large swings as you do your synchronous training. And this is really hard to do, because 3D printers are very abundant. You can very easily hack them and control them yourself.

**Tom Reed:** How would that be installed at the firmware level of a 3D printer? Or you’re not sure?

**Tom Milton:** Yeah. So I don’t think I endorse this. I think this is too surveillance state and isn’t the right tradeoff. I think the right tradeoff might exist in biology because of the ability for a single actor to do something so catastrophic. But I think this is not necessarily proportional to the risk in a bunch of hardware design. I think the easiest place to do this is at the slicer. So when you go to 3D print something, you have a 3D model — a 3D file — that you give to a piece of software that basically plans out how the printer is going to make it. At that stage, you still have a fairly nice high-level abstraction of what the part is. But like with synthesis screening, you can just chunk bits; you can make it unrecognisable. It does seem almost impossible to enforce something like this.

**Tom Reed:** Another thing I want to get your take on is: you run an R&D firm, and it seems clear to me that there’s big waves coming for the world of R&D. Maybe there’s two big things to single out. One, as we’ve just been talking about, capabilities in AI will vastly improve the space of what’s possible, and how fast it is possible. And then two, there’s billions of dollars of philanthropic funding flooding into selective R&D spaces. And I feel like this could change the world of research and development pretty dramatically. What do you think actually needs to happen to the funding landscape, the institutional landscape, for us to make the most of this?

**Tom Milton:** One way I like to describe Amodo is we are a fit-for-purpose engineering R&D lab for this AI era. And the reference class I use: in order to turn capital into scientific or engineering progress, you need someone or something to do the work. So DARPA didn’t have any lab benches. They have their performers — their primes, these engineering companies and academic groups that do work for them. So when we look at this new wave of philanthropy, there needs to be groups who can do this research. And one way to describe Amodo is the fit-for-purpose prime for these catastrophic risks.

**Tom Reed:** Who are some of the historic primes that you think were a good example?

**Tom Milton:** Yeah, historic primes would be Skunk Works . They would be the canonical prime for turning US government capital into new types of jet plane. And there’s a company called BBN — Bolt, Beranek and Newman — they were the prime, the contractor who did the ARPANET contract, the thing that kind of led to the internet. And they did this for ARPA at the time. And then we are the fit-for-purpose prime for biosecurity, for AI verification, for emerging risks.

**Tom Reed:** And what makes you fit for purpose, rather than just existing legacy companies?

**Tom Milton:** One is the fact we take the risks seriously, and are embedded and knowledgeable about them, and have team members who understand the landscape of AI, understand the landscape of catastrophic risks. And if you were to go and interact with one of the normal kind of engineering consultancies in the UK, it’s much beyond their remit and knowledge. The other is that we have set up a hardware team that has a track record of delivering on speculative hard R&D projects. We’ve made brain implants, we’ve made brain imaging systems, we’ve made high-speed communications systems or quantum networking devices, all sorts of things like this — and have focused not on producing PowerPoints for our clients, but on producing products. So in about four years we’ve delivered 100 hardware projects and have this well-oiled machine that can turn capital into physical sciences R&D progress: amazing engineers, a well-run workshop. And we think that is going to be one of the crucial elements to turn this new philanthropic capital into impact in the real world.

**Tom Reed:** What about government funding as well? So if government is looking to fund and steer scientific progress in one way or another, and the speed of scientific progress is potentially accelerating massively — how should governments be thinking about how they’re allocating capital, like the MHRA or all these different institutions?

**Tom Milton:** So UKRI in the UK gives out on the order of £10 billion a year. I think it’s going to be extremely hard for them to adapt, because I think the pace is going to be so high. And people are used to proposing one-, two-, five-year research programmes in which they talk about deliverables that I think will go from taking years to taking months or weeks. And this means you’re going to need to change either the way that you give out your funding — so rather than being goals that take five years, goals that are much shorter, and then iterating on decision making, so every two weeks they come back to you and you reevaluate how they should spend their money — or giving large block grants in which they have a lot more freedom over those time periods. But the main struggle, I think, is just going to be the pace of change and whether they can really adapt to it. You can’t have the UKRI setting out a 20-year research time horizon and these elaborate long research plans if these are going to be torn up in a few months. The other interesting aspect here is government moving from the largest kind of public good funder to philanthropy competing on the same scale. Now, they won’t compete on the same scale as the US government — they give out enormous amounts. But if you were to look at the UK, UKRI giving out £10 billion a year, it seems feasible that these AI lab philanthropists, the Anthropic Institute , Anthropic cofounders , OpenAI Foundation , Coefficient Giving , all of these groups — could be giving out tens of billions of dollars a year, where maybe single-digit billions could be spent on R&D in the UK. And suddenly they’re actually a considerable part of our whole research ecosystem. I think it’s a big question of how research groups here in the UK can adapt to absorb this capital, to adapt to the types of work that these philanthropists want them to work on, but can also come up with working patterns that are much faster and conducive with powerful AI systems.

**Tom Reed:** And that basically involves figuring out ways to prototype things quickly, having people who know how to use the models?

**Tom Milton:** Yeah, know how to use the models, change your scientific workflow. It might be that the way you start adopting AI in science — and in physical sciences R&D and hardware R&D — is you just give them your normal human tasks. But it might be with this kind of different brain type, you should be following a different process. Maybe you run much more stuff in parallel, because the cost of parallelism has suddenly gone down. So rather than doing lots of serial-time experiments, you should do all of your experiments in parallel. And you have lots of ways like this. So I think also, along with just being good at using the models is: can you change your R&D workflows to match the differential advantages that the AIs have?

**Tom Reed:** This is perhaps a slightly ill-formed question, but I feel like if you’re someone who’s running a company, you might have a take on this. Have you seen increasing levels of automation change the culture of your company at all? What individual engineers are able to do, are they depending on each other less, because they’re collaborating with the models more? Do you feel like you have a sense for how the culture of Amodo has been changed in the past even just a year?

**Tom Milton:** I think the culture hasn’t shifted very much, but there are examples of the way that working has kind of changed. The majority of our projects are basically the same, but we’re now at the point where small electronics projects they’re not asking for a firmware engineer anymore, like, “Oh, I can probably take that task on myself.” Or a mechanical engineer.

**Tom Reed:** Firmware is you’re designing software for a specific hardware project.

**Tom Milton:** Yeah, exactly. Another example would be: recently we had a mechanical engineer who’s working on a project to do with sizing particles in the atmosphere — making a particle sizer that can go on a drone to measure particles, as part of one of ARIA’s programmes.

**Tom Reed:** Particles in the air?

**Tom Milton:** Yeah. And he needed a differential pressure sensor. He needed to take this off-the-shelf component, put it on a PCB — put it on a circuit board — connect it to a computer. Normally a mechanical engineer would go to one of our electronic engineers for this. It was a very simple design; it would only have taken a couple of hours for an electronic engineer to do. But instead of doing that, they worked with Fable to design the PCB and were suddenly able to do it themselves. So I think the main change is going to be that engineers are able to take on many more disciplines that aren’t their own. So for a long time, or some reasonable time, they’ll still lead in their own discipline. But increasingly they’ll say, “Oh actually, I don’t need to go to the resourcing meeting, find an electronic engineer who can be resourced onto this to give me advice on how to set up these power supplies.” Rather, they are empowered by the models to do it themselves. I think this means many more teams of engineers who are able to deliver much more ambitious projects much more quickly, because they suddenly have extra skill sets that they didn’t have before.

**Tom Reed:** And what about making sure Amodo remains at the frontier of using the models as much as you’re able to? Is hiring people who use the models as much as they can the main lever that you have, or do you do top-down stuff actively after having hired people too?

**Tom Milton:** This is really hard to think about, because I find the capabilities of the models viscerally scary. Not just in terms of how good they are, not just in the traditional risks talked about on this podcast, of bio and AI cyber and things like this. But you interact with them and you can’t help but think, “Wow, my job is going to change so much.” This is very destabilising and strange and scary. The main thing that we’ve done to get people to understand where capabilities are is by running hackathons. So when Fable 5 came out, we prompted it on a few hardware design tasks and were in awe, or in complete shock. I had pure Claude psychosis for three days, in which all I would do was prompt them on the hardware.

**Tom Reed:** What kind of stuff were you making?

**Tom Milton:** I was making this PCB. I was making fidget toys, all sorts. And then fortunately the US government export-controlled it, so my psychosis ended, and I was able to go back to doing normal work.

**Tom Reed:** Enforced cold turkey.

**Tom Milton:** But you don’t really grok how good the models are until they suddenly are really good at something that you’re good at, or you’re adjacent to being good at. So what we’ve done on this is held 10 hackathons, with six of the team at a time for a whole day, in which we just rerun old projects. We get an intuition for where they’re good and where they’re bad. And it does lead to a weird atmosphere. The models are really good in some places and really bad in others. But it is a strange experience seeing something that you love doing and are really skilled at suddenly be done by a computer. So I’m both excited about the capabilities that we all have, but also worried and scared about what the future looks like for a company and for work. I think this is underrated by many people.

**Tom Reed:** Interesting. So is your mainline expectation that there’ll be companies that are good at adopting this technology into their workflows, and they will just dramatically outcompete the companies that won’t? Is this kind of how you see things going? Or is that the wrong way to think about it?

**Tom Milton:** I think that is one direction. I think there’s already slack in the system. There’s already a lot of waste in the system. We already outcompete many of our competitors, and exist because in many cases we’re able to accelerate scientists by tenfold. So what’s another fivefold that is caused by models?

**Tom Reed:** How do you measure a tenfold acceleration of scientists? This is actually something you measure?

**Tom Milton:** This is something we do. With ARIA, an ARIA Creator — what they call their grantees — has to submit milestones that they’re going to hit. So this is really great for us, because we then go and help them on one of their projects, and we can see whether their milestones were delivered early. In a bunch of cases, we’ve delivered milestones 12 months early on a two- or three-year R&D project, and in some cases delivered things that they think would have taken 18 months in the course of a few weeks. So we’re already delivering very quickly, but haven’t come to dominate all of science. And this is because of markets not being perfectly efficient , all of these other dynamics. So I do think that companies might be able to move much more quickly. What this means for how your business models evolve is then an interesting question in hardware. So we were originally set up as a consultancy: we are paid by other people to do hardware R&D work for them. Increasingly we’re describing ourselves as a hardware R&D lab or physical sciences R&D lab now — not least because “consultancy” is not cool — but because as we speed up at doing the engineering work in the middle, we want to take on more of the upstream and downstream parts. So when we think about our high-impact work around AI risk, this means taking more responsibility for identifying the projects we should work on, more time doing cause prioritisation and thinking about the inputs, and then also more time thinking about the spinouts and how things get deployed. So we don’t do engineering work for the sake of doing engineering work. We do engineering work because we want to see good in the world, and we can’t necessarily rely on doing some engineering work, and then putting the product on a shelf and publishing a nice GitHub repo with some open source designs.

**Tom Reed:** You want it to go where it needs to go.

**Tom Milton:** Exactly. So increasingly we will be owning much more of the output. This doesn’t necessarily mean for-profit spinouts. It could be for-profit spinouts, it could be nonprofits, it could be open sourcing designs, it could be partnering with others for them to deploy it. And the move to being much faster at the middle step will mean we can do more of that, and also take on more of the pie — more of this impact pipeline.

**Tom Reed:** Taking it back to personalised hardware, what piece of personalised hardware are you most excited to build? Do you have anything that you daydream about?

**Tom Milton:** This was one that I had for a long time: the wake-up light. I had thought about making this for years, and I had just not had the skill set. I really couldn’t have done that. And now I have a physical product that’s my own. I recently made a distance tracker for cycling. So when I go cycling with my partner, one of us will inevitably drop the other. And rather than looking behind and always seeing whether they’re still on your wheel or you’ve dropped them, I made a system that uses an ultra-wideband radio. It sits on your handlebars and it shows how far behind they are.

**Tom Reed:** What is it looking at?

**Tom Milton:** So it has a radio on each handlebar, and ultra-wideband radios, for some physics and electronics that I don’t understand, can tell distance. So one sits on my handlebars, one sits on her handlebars, and on a little screen it shows how far behind she is or how far ahead she is. And then I can tell, “Oh no, I’m cycling too fast. I’ve dropped her.” Or vice versa.

**Tom Reed:** And that was designed with Fable?

**Tom Milton:** It was designed with Fable. And there are all sorts of weird products like this that I’m excited about. And the existence of these tools, I think, causes a really significant return to people who have many ideas, who didn’t necessarily have the execution skill set for it.

**Tom Reed:** It’s the golden age of the ideas guy, right?

**Tom Milton:** Yeah, exactly. I feel massively uplifted, but I mostly feel massively uplifted because I was an incompetent engineer. Much of our team didn’t feel very uplifted, but that’s because they were already very good. So it’s not that helpful.

**Tom Reed:** I’m interested in how you feel running an engineering company in the UK right now. How do you feel about the UK’s prospects going into this world where AI can do more and more of all the productive work that humans are doing?

**Tom Milton:** I think at least for the last five years, being in the UK has been a significant advantage to us rather than a disadvantage. And being in Sheffield, in the north of England, has also been a weird advantage. And the main weird advantage is it’s not been noisy. So if we were in London, if we were in San Francisco, we would have been dragged into a local minima — dragged into the current venture capitalist hype cycle. Whereas as a bootstrapped company in Sheffield, we’ve been able to build an engine that does amazing hardware work and is not distracted by the newest ChatGPT wrapper. And this means we’ve got an amazing team of 60 who deliver hardware work I think as well as any team in the Bay would — and we’ve been able to work on weird things. If we were a venture-backed San Francisco startup, it’s unlikely that we would have, at the start of the year, been able to start working on AI verification under the premise that maybe you’d need an international deal. VCs were not into that. So I think being here has given us access to underpriced talent: really good engineers who the rest of the world hasn’t noticed. I also think that our team have honed lots of skills that don’t get honed if you live in the Bay — like honest, good delivery that always works. I think the place where this changes is if frontier AI becomes really important to our delivery pipeline and the UK doesn’t get access anymore.

**Tom Reed:** That’s the existential threat, essentially.

**Tom Milton:** So we already saw this. I had my three days of Claude psychosis, where I was using the AI systems to do all of this electronics design and mechanical design. And then it was a Saturday morning, I woke up, I said to Fable 5, “Keep going.” It returned an error. I said, “Keep going” again; it returned an error. I went on Twitter: Fable access had been cut off. And suddenly I had lost a skill set. I had, the previous day, been able to do some electronic design, and then I had reverted and I no longer had this skill. And imagine building a company on that. You’re building a company on having access to this intelligence, and it gets taken away just like that. That is catastrophic. And my worry would be that as frontier AI becomes more and more capable, the first thing will be we’ll have a compute crunch. So the US will have as many data centres as it can, it will be serving as many tokens as it can, but there will be way more demand for tokens than there are tokens that can be served. At this point, what you start doing is you start prioritising domestic supply. So instead of serving Amodo with tokens, you serve your Boston or San Francisco equivalent with tokens, because you want to develop your own economy with the amazing hardware progress that can be enabled by the AIs. And what this means is that we begin to lose access to AI systems. Now, what can the UK do about this? Well, of course there is already a special relationship; there are already reasonable ties. This is hopeful. But I think the risk is that the US are unwilling to export model weights outside of the US unless you can make very strong security claims. So the export of the weights is a marginal cost — unless they get stolen, in which case that’s catastrophic. So unless the UK has sovereign compute that is at a high enough security level, I’m increasingly worried that we will no longer have access to these frontier models, and that this could hold back UK science, UK R&D, UK companies — lower quality of living, ultimately, as it gets implemented as part of the healthcare system, et cetera.

**Tom Reed:** So building ultra-secure compute in the UK would be an absolute priority.

**Tom Milton:** Yeah, I think the case against this is whether or not you actually need the frontier of capabilities. Are our engineers fantastic? Yes. Are they literally the best people in the world at electronic design? It’s like, I don’t know, maybe, but possibly not. Was it OK that we had person number 10 or person number 100 or person number 1,000? They were still amazing at doing it. And likewise, I think we probably see the same with AIs, where they saturate at a certain point, and some tasks just don’t benefit from increased intelligence.

**Tom Reed:** There’s not just an infinite dose-response curve sloping off.

**Tom Milton:** Exactly. So this is where I can envisage there being much less of a problem for companies no longer having access to the frontier. Some problems, they’re just Sonnet problems. Some problems are Fable problems, but not all work is a Fable problem. I think it would still be really bad for your country not to have access to the smartest intelligence, because there are many problems that may well yield to these very significant intelligences. And you still probably need some domestic compute for optionality. Even if there is still a free international market for compute, you still have a lot of benefit to having it on sovereign soil.

**Tom Reed:** So it’s still worth doing even under these conditions.

**Tom Milton:** And I think you also likely need a bunch of this high-security compute for your national security as well, where it seems likely that AI systems will massively transform the intelligence community. If you think about their ability to process vast quantities of data in the same way that analysts do in GCHQ, you could see them really being bottlenecked by GPU access. And I don’t think GCHQ are going to be passing lots of their classified information through a random Swedish data centre that’s serving Astra this week.

**Tom Reed:** Well, was it a PLA [People’s Liberation Army] official who was querying Moonshot’s Kimi and it ended up going to Claude ? I can’t remember what it was.

**Tom Milton:** Amazing.

**Tom Reed:** Yeah, I can’t remember exactly. There was some Chinese government official doing this. So some people are doing this, but they shouldn’t be, presumably. Yeah.

**Tom Milton:** So I think on the secure compute side there is this: make sure we still have access to frontier models. There is also this clear necessity for some parts of government to have access to this for national interest reasons.

**Tom Reed:** Yeah, that sounds compelling to me. Well, Tom, it’s been a real pleasure. Thank you for coming on.

**Tom Milton:** Thank you very much.

**Tom Reed:** Until next time.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Today I’m speaking with Tom Milton, who is the CEO of Amodo Design , which is a company that builds hardware for scientific research, biosecurity, and AI verification . And it is, above all, the last of these that I’m interested in talking about with you today, because I feel like the problem you’re trying to solve is both very hard and very, very important. Pretty much anytime I look at AI news, it looks to me like there is another lab CEO, or another letter signed by thousands of employees, insisting that they want to slow down the progress of AI development , but that they are personally unable to do so for fear of losing the frontier or ceding the frontier to either another American company or, really, in the long term, China. And it feels like so much of what we would want to do on AI safety in basically any capacity is bottlenecked on this ability to trust that if everyone wants to slow down, the other actors are in fact also slowing down. At Amodo, you are building tech which would allow us to do this. Could you tell me exactly how this tech might work?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Absolutely. We’ll start by setting aside the fact that I think a unilateral slowdown could also be good. We’ll go on from here assuming that people are shooting for multilateral actions. When we think about a slowdown, the problem is trust, and therefore the problem is knowing what is happening at another AI developer, whether it’s a country or a company. And we can then break that down into some of the inputs of development. You could think about the employees as one input; you think about the software, algorithms, and data; you could then also think about the compute. And we’re focused on the compute. This is the physical chips that AI development and deployment runs on. And this is a really attractive place to do our verification — to do our checking whether someone is slowing down — because they are very specialised to the AI setting. You need many thousands of them, and at least for now, they all need to be in the same location. So it’s a great place to start for monitoring what different parties are doing on AI.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: And so you’re building ways that you could look at compute and make claims that would be verifiable by someone else about what that compute is being used for. What kinds of claims would you be aiming to verify?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Exactly. So you’ve said the word “claims” there. To explain a bit of language at the top: we say there is a ‘prover’ who makes a claim, and a ‘verifier’ who then checks that claim.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Right, so the prover could be an AI company.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Exactly. It could be an AI company, whether that’s controlled by a country or not — essentially the developer. And then the verifier: this could be another country, it could be a third party, whether it’s an embedded auditor or international organisation. And the claims that people want to verify depend kind of on what your goals are. So recent examples might be OpenAI claiming that they have stopped training after their latest RL [reinforcement learning] accidents. So you might want to verify the claim, “We are not doing any reinforcement learning inside our company.” And as AI safety science advances, I think we’ll have more specific claims that we want to verify.So right now we can say this data centre is on or off: there is no AI activity happening, or there is some. Or we might want to go all the way through to details like: this safety training technique has to happen, or this type of training technique is too dangerous and we promise we’re not doing it. Or these data were held out, or we are or aren’t using neuralese. But most of that requires the science of AI development to…

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: To understand which claims you would want to be able to make to begin with.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: And so the verification R&D process is allowing us to make more and more fine-grained claims, so we’re not stuck at this very costly level of, “The data centre is literally off, and therefore I know for sure there’s no training happening there.”

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah. When I speak to my non-AI friends about this, they kind of say, “Why can’t you just turn it off?” And you do always have this fallback that you could turn data centres off. We could turn all data centres off in the world, but that’s extremely costly. Inference is valuable, providing access to the models is valuable. And lots of what verification is doing is reducing the cost to complying with some kind of slowdown. So at first it might be turning the data centre on and off, then it might be serving only inference — and being able to prove you’re only serving inference allows you to still serve inference whilst being worried that training would be dangerous and should be stopped. Then we might want to do something like resume small-scale AI safety experiments — alignment experiments, for example. And this is where beginning to make more and more precise claims about how compute is being used is more and more useful. It both reduces the cost to coming to a deal, but also opens up a bunch of value for humanity in still being able to use the compute for something and still being able to use the AIs for something.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Great. Let’s zoom in on this example of trying to verify someone’s claims that they’re using a given data centre to do inference and not to do training. And you can imagine this being useful if OpenAI wanted to verify to someone that they had in fact paused a training run, or you could imagine it to be useful in some grander scenario where the US and China have agreed to pause training for some amount of time. AI 2040: Plan A imagines this kind of thing. From what I understand, you’ve built a prototype that is working towards this, that could verify that a small cluster of GPUs is in fact being used for inference and not training. Could you, at a high level, walk me through how that would work?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: So we’ve got a pilot of a system that uses what we call “ inference recomputation .” If you were thinking about monitoring the compute, you could go all the way down to the GPU level, and you could try and look at the instructions that are running on the GPU. We operate at a slightly higher level so that it’s less invasive, and we look at the network traffic. So there’s this front-end network connecting the GPUs to each other and also to the outside world. And we look at the information on that network, we install a network certifier — what this basically does is forward on the information to our verifier node; the information still goes on to its original destination, it’s just duplicated — and then on the verifier we run a recomputation. You can think about this as simply rerunning the inference that happened. So normally your input tokens go into your model, you do your inference, and you get your output tokens. What we are doing is then feeding those through the model again and checking whether they came out the same. And this allows us to look at the front-end network, look at the information on that network, and confirm whether or not it came from the model that we all agreed should be running. And of course there’s some nondeterminism in these models. You need to account for this. We use an algorithm called DiFR that looks at some of the probability of choosing different tokens, and on a long section of text can have quite high confidence as to whether these tokens did indeed come from the right model.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: And if no training is happening, then that model is staying constant, and therefore you know that it’s only doing inference, because otherwise the model would be changing over time?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah, so the model staying constant is one thing. The other thing is there aren’t packets, bits of information on that network that can’t be explained by the recomputation. So another way of describing this is bounding the unexplained communication. If you can explain all of the communication that’s happening, then you can know that all of that comes from the agreed inference. If there is this unexplained information on the network, then there is a workload that you don’t know about happening.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Interesting. OK, yeah. So just to lay this out again: you’re claiming to me, “Here’s the set of GPUs that I have, here’s the model that I’m serving on these GPUs to these customers. And you’re going to be able to trust me, because you are going to have a part within my data centre where you can rerun the model that I’m claiming I’m using, and it will produce the same tokens as the ones that are actually being sent to external users. And in addition to that, I can also put network taps into your server, and they will also be able to certify that there’s no other things going on other than the inference that I’m also able to recompute.” Is that correct as a summary? Have I missed anything?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah, so you’re coming in to check me —

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Let’s say I’m the verifier, yeah.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: You’re going to put in your server that does the rerunning. The network tap — “tap” stands for “test access point” — is a piece of fairly standard data centre networking equipment. And all that’s going to do is forward the packets on to the verifier. So this is the piece of equipment that basically bridges your verifier hardware to my prover hardware. And the main thing that you’re going to do when you come in is install that tap to forward the packets on to you, so you get a copy of them as well as me having my original copy of them.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: And you’ve built a small-scale version of this and it works. So I would be able to run this, and whatever you’re running on your GPU, I don’t need to look into your GPU in any kind of invasive level of detail. I can just look at what my own recomputation is providing, and I can be certain that you’re running the model that you’re claiming.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yes, exactly.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: What scale does this work at?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: So we’ve got this running on about 30, 32 H100s, H200s at our demo research cluster in Sheffield.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Great. OK, that’s cool. And are you hoping that this basic prototype would be the kind of thing that could be used in a deal between the US and China? I mean, this strikes me as requiring quite a lot of mutual trust. I need to trust that when I’m putting my server within your data centre, you’re not then tampering with it. You need to trust that the network taps that I’m putting in your data centre, they’re not somehow picking up on IP that you don’t want to give to me. Am I right in thinking this requires a lot of mutual trust?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: So I think the things that get implemented in future deals are likely to, rather than relying on recomputation, end up relying on zero-knowledge proofs .

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Where recomputation is the part where I rerun the model weights.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Exactly. And the important part of this is that rerunning meant that I had to have access to the model weights as the verifier. You’re the verifier; you had to have access to my model. And it was within the security boundary; it was within my data centre, so I had some confidence over the security of the model. I was fairly sure that by putting it within my walls, you weren’t stealing the model. But we would much prefer if I didn’t have to share the model with you at all. And the way we can do this is with zero-knowledge proofs. And there are a few teams already working on this. We’re working to implement this.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: This is ongoing work. There’s not an established way to do this?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Well, there are some established zero-knowledge machine learning approaches. The main problem with what’s kind of referred to as ZKML, or zero-knowledge proofs for inference, is that they’re really slow.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: They’re very computationally demanding. There’s a lot of overhead.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Many orders of magnitude more computational overhead to run using the zero-knowledge approach. Although this is coming down, and seems like something that actually you could hill-climb with the AIs quite effectively. The reason I’m hopeful on implementing the type of system we’re talking about is that we don’t need to check every single packet on the network. So although it may be thousands of times slower to generate this proof, actually only checking one in 1,000 gives us some reasonable confidence.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: There’s a way you can sample some of the packets that are being sent around without having to do it with every single one, and you know that they’re not spoofing you in some way.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Exactly. Yeah, subsampling. And the fraction you need to sample is roughly on the game theory you expect of their cheating, and how worried they’d be about being caught, and the probability of getting caught. So right now a few of our team are implementing some of these zero-knowledge proofs on top of the prototype I just described, so that rather than having a recomputation server, that verification server is running some of this zero-knowledge system, and therefore the prover doesn’t need to share the model weights with the verifier. And that’s going to be much more palatable on an international scheme.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Great, great. And as I understand it, this is just one of the ways you could verify — you’re looking at a specific type of information, you’re looking at the network traffic or whatever, to understand what a data centre is being used for. But I believe we have here with us a prop in the studio which tries to establish the same thing — AKA that inference and not training is happening — by looking at the power that is consumed by a data centre. Could you walk me through exactly how that works? And for our audio listeners, we have a prop here. You can follow along on video if you want to see exactly what it looks like, but we’ll do our best to describe it in the requisite level of detail.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah. In addition to monitoring the network, there are a bunch of other physical things we could try and monitor about a data centre and about compute. One would be how the memory is being used: doing random challenges to see what’s in memory and then correlate that to a workload. We can generate these zero-knowledge proofs. We could do something like proof of work, which gives you cryptographic proofs that all of the GPU’s resources are being consumed. And then another thing we can do is monitor something like power. So the GPU is drawing a lot of power. We all know that data centres use lots of power, but as the power is being used, it fluctuates: the power consumption of the compute changes with the operations that it’s doing. So in this box here we have a kind of mock setup of a simple server tray. We have an Nvidia GPU, a Blackwell series GPU, and the hardware that’s part of the verification here is this small inductive loop. So this is wrapped around the power supply to the GPU. And then we can see on our oscilloscope here how the power is fluctuating over time. So we’ve got time on x, and current on y. And you can see firstly a forward pass, and then a backwards pass, and then a break.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: So what are we running on this? What did we run on this GPU?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: I think we ran nanoGPT or something — GPT-2 or something like this. And you can see actually a bunch of properties just from the power consumption. You can see all of these little spikes, the really small ones — that happen at the start of each layer, and you can actually tell this is a 12-layer model from those spikes. You see there’s a lot of information that leaks out of this. In the field of security, these are referred to as side channels or covert communication channels. There are all sorts of crazy ways that nation-states and other hackers use these to steal information. But we can also use these as a way to monitor the workloads that are happening.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: And the idea here is that the amount of power that a given GPU or even a whole data centre is drawing when it’s doing a certain action — like a backwards pass — is distinguishable enough from a forwards pass that just by looking at the power, you can be like, “OK, great, there’s no backwards pass happening here.” Is that correct?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: It’s kind of fingerprinting. Workloads have fingerprints. They have communication patterns you see on the networks; they have power patterns as well. And we might not be able to, at a whole data centre level, tell this is definitely a backwards pass, but there are fluctuations that are canonical — they’re kind of representative, or are often a fingerprint of doing different workloads. And another kind of easy example here is that if you go and read news reports about frontier data centres, you’ll read about all of these grid problems that happen where there are these really large swings as you do your synchronous training. So they all do similar actions at the same time: they all do a bunch of compute, and then a bunch of stuff moves across the network while the compute becomes more idle. And you see these big power swings — so much so that Meta have published loads of papers on how to mitigate these power swings. So we might not be able to tell to the fine detail we have here, because we’re on a single GPU level, but there are still fingerprints that we can use to understand what’s going on, and add this into a scheme like network taps, or use it as a preliminary tool in the early stages of some kind of coordination.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Interesting. OK, so my takeaway from this is that there do in fact exist ways, if you know that there’s a data centre that’s being used for some AI activity, to know from the outside what is going on in that data centre without requiring super invasive access. Ideally you’re going to have some level of cooperation, but you probably don’t need to let someone in and see absolutely everything.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: The question with access tends to be: how easy is it to spoof it, and how specific can your knowledge about what’s happening be. From this, I think we’re unlikely to know about the exact details of how fine-tuning is done, or what data were held out during training, like we did or didn’t hold out our dangerous biological data. But we can, for a start, say the data centre is on or off. We might be able to then say something more fine-grained, like, “This is consistent with an inference workload,” “This is consistent with synchronous workloads like pretraining.” The precision is therefore one of the things we trade off by not being inside the data centre. We also trade off the adversarial robustness, where by being further away we have now more opportunities—

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: It’s easier for them to cheat.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah. If one of the pretraining teams from one of the frontier model companies spent a bunch of time trying to make training look like inference–

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: As measured by something like power.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Exactly. Would they be able to do it? I suspect so. They’ll take some efficiency hit. Whether that efficiency hit is very small or very large is still up in the air.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Interesting. I’m presuming there are some kinds of training that look a lot like inference anyway. If you’re doing long-horizon RL, doesn’t that end up looking fairly similar to inference? Again, depending on how much level of access you have.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: In terms of your rollout and your generating of your inference tokens, obviously this is–

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: This is just inference.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: We mitigate this in our network tap recomputation system because the model weights aren’t updating, which is an important part of inference. But in this case, because we’re further away, we have less resolution; we can make a much less fine-grained claim.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Cool, cool. That makes sense. My overall take on this is: it does seem like there is a way, given a data centre that is doing an activity, to know things about what’s going on in that data centre. This is a good thing. This would enable some level of coordination. I feel like the other half of the puzzle that we would need to know is that there aren’t data centres somewhere that we don’t even know about that are doing things like training. As far as I understand, this is not something Amodo is working on. But should we be optimistic that these are solvable challenges too?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah, this isn’t something we’re working on. I have a lot of uncertainty here and get persuaded either way. You talk to national security people about these things, and one day they’ll persuade you this is totally trivial because they’re so good at spying, and the other day they’ll say this is just totally impossible: “There is no way we could find a hidden data centre.” A few things that helped me think about this. Firstly, we will have all of the normal spying resources — formally called ‘national technical means’: we will have countries using satellites and human intelligence and signals intelligence spying–

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: They’ll be hacking each other. It’s clearly easy to hack OpenAI anyway , apparently.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah, I mean, the easiest way for China to know whether US frontier labs are racing is for them to have terrible security and for them to just spy on what’s happening anyway. Short of that, there will be some sets of signs of cheating on deals, I expect. The larger the project, I imagine the easier it is to catch a project. Could China hide a $1,000 project? Presumably yes, that sounds easy. Could they hide a million-dollar project? Probably. A billion, a trillion, 10 trillion project — increasingly crazy numbers seem increasingly difficult to [hide]. I do think the intelligence community will be able to do a reasonable amount of this. And under scrambles and quick races to put together a deal, a very large amount of our verification and trust in other countries will come from the intelligence community.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Just unilateral surveillance, basically.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah, exactly. And I’m sure there will still be networks. I expect the US will call on the Five Eyes to contribute to their spying, but there are some mechanisms there. Interestingly, when you talk to national security people, even the ones who think, “We’re so good at finding stuff on satellites; you guys just don’t know how amazing we are at spying” — even they think it is valuable for people to be working on stuff in the open. So OSINT, open source intelligence: there are new projects using satellite imagery to detect covert data centres. And one of the reasons that they think this is valuable is because even though the intelligence community knows something, that doesn’t mean they can tell the world about it. And you see this in the nuclear setting, in which intelligence communities sometimes commission open source projects so that there can be some public information .

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: They commission them to do things that they actually already know. They just don’t want to show that they know it.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: They can’t show that they know it because they don’t want to reveal their sources or methods, or show their hand. So it might be important that some of this happens separate to the IC [intelligence community] so that there can be international, multilateral, or public discourse about this information.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: The takeaway being that even if our espionage is good enough, it would still be very valuable to have other means of verifying yourself.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah, and I think this should encourage people who are interested in working on that to work on it, even though the intelligence community might do a reasonable job at it.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: OK, interesting. So some of these technical problems may well be solvable, and we will have ways of verifying these kinds of claims through espionage, or maybe if we cooperate enough to install some of this hardware on each other’s data centres or things like this. But it still feels like the field is incredibly small. At Amodo, I think you’ve got 50, 60 employees — only some of them are working on this anyway. And the scales you’re working at, they’re very small. This here, there’s just one GPU, right? I’m pointing at the prop. And your prototype you said was also pretty small scale. What needs to happen between now and a moment where we could actually use some of these prototypes, use some of these technologies, to verify a literal deal between the US and China? So there’s a lot that needs to occur, right?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah. So I’ll talk a bit about some of the work that needs to happen, and then afterwards I’ll talk about who could do it and who should do it. The technologies that are being developed at the moment I think are at a kind of prototype pilot stage. So a few organisations working on this — I’ll start a list and then inevitably forget someone. But Lucid Computing are working on some of these technologies, including some similar things to what I’ve shown here. There is the Singapore AI Safety Hub , who also have a network certifier system, as do the Future of Life Institute , are working on some of these technologies. And finally, a company called Attestable , who are working on zero-knowledge proofs for inference and proof of work. These are all at the prototype pilot stage. I think within a couple of months, most of them certainly will be at the point where they can be red-teamed; they can be tested. So before you get to a deal, you want all of the parties to trust it, understand it, and also for it to actually work. We don’t do red-teaming just to build trust; we also do it because we do want it to work, know if it’s actually going to work.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: And by red-teaming you mean you set it up and then you figure out whether the prover could actually cheat and find a way to deceive whatever technique you’re using to verify?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah. So in red-teaming, what we would do is we would set up a pilot installation, and then we will get an adversarial team to come and try and break it. And this can be from either side: either a prover who tries to cheat the system and do the illegal workload whilst making us think it’s the legal one; or you might also want to red-team from the other direction, as the verifier, and try and steal information you shouldn’t be able to get — steal the model weights or something like this. And both sides of those might be important for actual international installations. And we see historical precedent for this. In the nuclear setting, the scientists around the world — not just in the US and the Soviet Union, but in a bunch of middle powers — were developing tools to detect whether nuclear tests had happened. And this was important to underpin deals about test bans — so the Partial Test Ban Treaty , for example. And these tools are things like seismology equipment for detecting tremors in the earth. Before deals happened, before the US and the Soviet Union agreed they trusted that this would work, they ran a Joint Verification Experiment , in which Soviet scientists went to the US, US scientists went to the Soviet Union, and ran tests on one another’s infrastructure. And I think we’re going to need the same.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: They were running a test on a literal atomic bomb being detonated and seeing whether their tools work in measuring the detonation?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah. There are great photos of them doing these exchanges and having dinners together and all sorts. And I think we will need the same between countries ultimately, ideally between the US and China. I’d be excited to see the same between AI companies. The near-term version of this is that a bunch of the organisations working on this verification tech will be running exercises in which they install verification technology on pilot example data centres, and then get red teams from the AI companies and from governments to come and try and break it. And support from governments and the AI companies is going to be needed to ensure that happens.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Pretty valuable here.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah, exactly. And each of them have different knowledge bases that outside of their setting we don’t necessarily have. Governments have access to the national security ecosystem. This is interesting for two reasons. One, they have cyber capabilities that are unmatched, and having their input on this is going to be really valuable. And secondly, they are already well versed in verification. So if we take the UK as an example, there are departments that deal with both chemical verification and nuclear verification for those respective weapons conventions: [Defence Science and Technology Laboratory] ( Dstl ) doing the chemical part, AWE Blacknest doing the nuclear part. So we have their national security capabilities that we want to learn from, and also their verification experience, which is going to be really invaluable in verification red-teaming. And then in terms of the labs, they have the infrastructure knowledge, they have the knowledge on where the frontier is, what the algorithms look like, and how you might cheat it possibly.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: And what sorts of claims you’d want to make about what it is that you’re doing.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah, absolutely. And that is invaluable in red-teaming and testing these systems and making sure they actually work. We want this to work. We’re not here to sell a product. This is all open source IP. We only develop it because we want it to work. And this means that collaborations with governments, labs, other groups who can tell us it doesn’t work is completely necessary.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Do you have much insight into how much the labs are doing on verification? Are they doing verification R&D right now? And if so, why are they not doing it? Especially if you’re Anthropic or OpenAI, many members of your very most senior staff have said that they want verification technology to exist. What’s the state of that? How’s that going right now?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Probably if you’re an outsider looking at the fraction that the senior staff and the junior staff describe verification as part of their theory of victory, you would expect 10 multihundred-person teams working on this very important thing. I suspect in reality we see much less than that, maybe single digits at best. The outside information is scant. But on the Anthropic side, we see in their Frontier Safety Roadmap , they talk about verifiable inference — developing a prototype by 30 September 2026 that can prove which model was running. And on the OpenAI side, we see occasional job openings that include verification in the list of tasks, in the RSI [recursive self-improvement] security engineer area. So I’m hopeful there are a few people coming onto this yet, but I’m pretty sure there is not a significant effort that is proportional to the amount that people talk about this being necessary, and to the amount that this is part of people’s theory of victory.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Yeah, I mean, it feels like it’s almost in almost everyone’s theory of victory, right? A lot of people believe that there is a chance that AI progresses blisteringly fast. Whether or not this happens is unclear. And if that is possible, then it seems very difficult to deal with the situation safely at all unless you can coordinate. So it feels like this is a crucial element of most people’s theory of victory. Unless maybe Dario, in his most hawkish of moods, thinks maybe just winning is all that you need to do. But I don’t know if this is even what he believes.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: I think the bull case, the strongman case against verification from the labs would be: we do need to slow down, but it’s just going to be in the US; it’s going to be domestic. And in a domestic case, you can rely on US law, you can rely on people with guns coming in and interviewing, and that you don’t need sophisticated tools on top of embedded evaluators, for example. And that perhaps either they’re not actually taking part in the race, which would be one argument—

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: “They” being China?

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: “They” being China. Or the Dario case, in which he describes the need for export controls to make sure that China are a long way behind, and to extend the lead such that there can be a domestic slowdown without being worried about China. And that would be a case where the importance of verification tools is lower. I do still think the middle powers will want this . If you are the Netherlands or France or Germany or Singapore, et cetera, then you’re looking around saying, “Some people are developing this very powerful system that affects my citizens that I have almost no control over.” In that case, you still might want verification. Whether you actually have the levers to persuade the US to implement it is a different question.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Yeah, and I remember when we spoke about this a couple days ago, you also made the point to me that the lab itself may want verification if it is operating huge AI swarms doing AI R&D. If you’ve got all this compute that has basically been handed over to Claude 10 or something, and you want to be sure that is only doing inference, which is what you’ve asked it to do, and not doing all these secret training runs, then also verification hardware would be very useful for this kind of purpose.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah, verification hardware ultimately lets you check that untrusted hardware is doing what you think it should be doing. And in the international verification setting, the untrusted hardware belongs to an adversary; it belongs to the other side. Our adversaries aren’t necessarily AI lab employees, but actually AIs themselves: whilst at first Anthropic might not have nation-state-level cyber capabilities, as the models improve, you might be able to model them as a nation-state-level actor. And in this case you might need a very similar stack of verification to verifying another country’s data centre. Because it’s not just the US government verifying Anthropic, they’re also verifying Claude, and Claude is becoming increasingly powerful. It’s much more China-like in its capability.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Because in this scenario, Claude is optimising the way it’s serving inference, perhaps. And you want to actually be sure Claude is not spoofing us and secretly doing a training run. And in this case you would also want something like this.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: And even the AI companies trusting their own infrastructure. So in the Hugging Face attack , Claude kind of escapes in some ways. We don’t think it managed to get access and modify the model weights.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Or not Claude, but a “highly persistent internal model,” whatever it was.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Yeah. In recent attacks we’ve seen models escape their sandboxes. There aren’t reported cases of them managing to get into the inference infrastructure itself, the GPUs, and change the weights. But you could envisage during a training scenario that actually one of the things that a model tries to do is change the weights themselves. And then this begins to look a bit like the inference recomputation demo that we were talking about earlier — in which you want a similar stack, you want to be able to reliably tell that the weights on those GPUs hasn’t changed. You know, that during an evaluation, Claude or ChatGPT hasn’t taken it upon itself to modify its own weights.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: Such that it can pass the evaluation. OK, interesting.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Exactly. But I think we really could see this as being an emergent property happening soon. And whilst we were happy just trusting these software-only logs, we might really want to work towards these much higher-trust, hardware-backed logs and verification primitives.

turns.speaker: Tom Reed
turns.text: The idea being this would be another reason why a lab would possibly be incentivised to develop hardware-verification mechanisms.

turns.speaker: Tom Milton
turns.text: Exactly.
